name: Omar Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Omar, thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential. Okay to start?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, go for it. I've got my coffee.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now it's two things. I subtitle Arabic documentaries into English for a subtitling agency that works for streaming services, and I do what's called transcreation for an advertising agency. Transcreation means rewriting an advert so it works in another culture, like making a perfume slogan land in the Gulf instead of just translating it. My day starts with an AI tool that transcribes the audio and times the subtitles, then I fix it line by line. Afternoons are calls with the ad agency, arguing about whether a word sounds too old-fashioned.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the arguing, honestly, because it's where the real thinking happens. What wears me out is dialect: a Moroccan fisherman and a Syrian grandmother in the same film, and the AI transcript is hopeless with both. I'm still learning, and the senior subtitler, Leila, catches things I miss every week. I'm fast because of the tools, but I'm not yet good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's kind of a relief, kind of a letdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a decent assistant that got oversold. I'd say the tools that work are the boring ones, like auto-timing subtitles. Online I'd probably post something like 'told you, the hype people owe us an apology', half as a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. I already use the tools better than most juniors, so in a plateau I keep that speed advantage and nobody replaces the job itself. My pay is above average because I'm fast, and I've got about a year's money saved plus index funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and push my setup further, maybe write little scripts to clean up the AI transcripts automatically. I'd ask the ad agency for more transcreation, because that pays twice what subtitles do. And I'd keep putting 500 a month into the index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Mildly smug, maybe. Mostly calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why index funds, and not something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want to think about it. A friend from university showed me how in my first year of freelancing. Putting money into an index fund every month is the one boring thing in my life I'm proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Translators who spend all day typing what a machine could draft. Even in a plateau, they get slower than the market. I'd worry about them, but I'd also tell them to learn the tools, kindly.

The tools that work are the **boring ones**, like auto-timing subtitles.
The hype people **owe us an apology**, half as a joke.
think: I keep my **speed advantage** and nobody replaces the job.
About **a year's money** saved plus index funds makes me secure.
do: Write small **scripts** to clean up AI transcripts automatically.
Ask the ad agency for more **transcreation**, which pays double.
Keep putting **500 a month** into the index fund.
S0.quote: Putting money into an index fund every month is the one boring thing in my life I'm proud of.
fieldNote: He's **tool-first**: AI is already the first step of his day.
His **pay edge** comes from speed, not yet from skill.
He's kind but firm that others should **learn the tools**.

steps.text: Write scripts that clean up AI subtitle transcripts
Ask the ad agency for more transcreation work
Keep putting 500 a month into an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. That's the one I'd bet on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the job is changing, not dying, and the translators who adapt will be fine. I'd probably post a guide on how to use the subtitle tools well. I'd say it in a positive way, because people panic otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, plain subtitling becomes a machine job with one human checker per ten films. I'd want to be that checker or the person managing them. Transcreation lasts longer, because it's taste and culture, but even that gets squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the subtitling agency for a junior project manager role, running the AI pipeline and the checkers. I'd learn every new tool as it comes, the same week. And I'd keep investing, maybe a bit more in the companies building these tools, as a hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit buzzing. I can see a path, but I know I'm not the only one looking at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else is looking at that path?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila, for one. The senior subtitler Leila is better than me at language and nearly as good with the tools. If there's one manager job, she gets it, and honestly she should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm moving up, not out. My mum would ask if it's still translation, and I'd say sort of. My dad would ask if it pays more, and I'd say yes, which ends the conversation.

**Transcreation** lasts longer, but even that gets squeezed.

steps.text: Apply for a junior project manager role at the subtitling agency

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then the pipeline doesn't need a manager either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper safety net, and fast, because a lot of good people are going to fall at once. I'd say it at work and online, without drama. I'm not a protest guy, but I'd sign things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, all my work is thinking work, so it's gone by 2028, manager job included. The AI would do the dialect better than Leila. What still needs a human for about three more years is anything on the ground, in person, with your hands and your face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start working as a fixer for documentary crews. A fixer is the local person who arranges access, drives, translates in person and keeps everyone out of trouble. I've subtitled enough of these films to know the crews, so I'd email three producers this month. I'd keep a year's savings untouched and move some of my index money into cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be thinking about it every night. But I'm someone who likes a plan, and I'd have one by the weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A fixer travels a lot. What does that change in your life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, a bit. I'd be away for weeks in places I've only seen on screen. I'm single and I've got no kids, so I'm exactly the person who can take that job, which feels lucky and lonely at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots arrive about three years after the AI. Does fixing survive that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe longer than most things. A robot can drive a van, sure. But nobody in a small fishing town lets a robot talk them into being filmed.

say: We need a proper **safety net**, fast, because many people fall at once.
I'm not a protest guy, but I'd **sign things**.
think: All my work is **thinking work**, so it's gone by 2028.
Work **on the ground**, in person, lasts about three more years.

fieldNote: He jumps to **in-person work** that uses both language and trust.
Being **single and childless** makes a travelling job possible.
Turns investments into **cash** for safety, a careful move for a risk-taker.

steps.text: Email three documentary producers about fixer work this month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, I can be smarter about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same about a safety net, but I'd add that five years is enough to retrain a lot of people if we start now. I'd say that to the other freelancers in my group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd squeeze the translation work for three years while it pays, then switch before 2031. Fixing would be my second job first and my main job later. The robots coming about three years after AGI gives on-the-ground work until roughly 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take fixer jobs in my holidays, two or three a year, starting next year, to build contacts. I'd do a driving and first-aid course for remote filming, which crews ask for. And I'd keep investing, 500 a month, because if AI is that strong, the companies using it will grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in an active way. More like training for a race than waiting for a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the companies will grow. Does it feel strange to profit from the thing that ends your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, a bit. But I'd rather own a tiny slice of the machine than just be replaced by it. That's not a philosophy, it's just maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up for those fixer trips?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My actual holidays, and probably a girlfriend if I had one. My friends already say I treat my calendar like a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do it properly: training, safety nets, all of it. I'd be the annoyingly upbeat one in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have six or seven good years in the language business, maybe as a project manager running AI pipelines. Then a move in my early thirties, which is normal anyway. It doesn't scare me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and chase the project manager role, using the tools to take on more projects. I'd keep investing. And I'd treat fixing as a someday plan, maybe one trip a year to keep the door open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, just a little. Mostly I'd be curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do differently with ten years that you wouldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd actually get good at dialects, for my own pride. Leila says you need ten years in this job before you can really hear the difference between two villages. I'd like to get there before the machines do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The forty-five-year-olds in 2036. I'll be thirty-seven and fine, probably. They'll be too young to stop and too old to start from scratch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd cope, I think, but a lot of people around me wouldn't, and that changes the world I'd be living in. What would help is a fast, simple safety net and travel visas that make it easy for fixers and crews to work across borders.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to dialects. If the machines learn a standard Arabic and everyone talks to them, the village words my grandmother used might just stop. I'd like someone to record them while there's still time.

headlineQuote: If the machines learn a standard Arabic and everyone talks to them, the village words my grandmother used might just stop.
portrait: Omar is a 27-year-old **Arabic-English** subtitler and advert transcreator who uses AI tools daily.
He's **fast but still learning**, and admits a senior colleague is better.
He saves and **invests** steadily, treating it as maths, not philosophy.
In faster AGI scenarios he'd become a **documentary fixer**, betting on in-person trust.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mostly for the people around him who wouldn't cope.
whatWouldHelp: **Visas** that let fixers and crews work easily across borders.
